puzzles.background: This Melbourne suburb's streets honor the leaders of the nation, from its earliest prime ministers to those who shaped modern Australia.
puzzles.reveal: It was Altona, where every street pays tribute to a prime minister.

rounds.clue: This wartime leader famously declared, 'We shall hold this country for the British people... we shall hold it as a trust for the British people. We shall hold it for the British Empire, and we shall hold it for the British race.'
rounds.tidbit: John Curtin was the only Australian prime minister to die in office during World War II, passing away just weeks before the war ended.
rounds.explainer: John Curtin served as Australia's 14th Prime Minister from 1941 to 1945, leading the nation through the darkest days of World War II. He famously turned to the United States for protection when Britain fell to the Japanese advance, a pivotal shift in Australian foreign policy. Curtin's leadership was marked by his unwavering commitment to the Australian people, and he is remembered as one of the nation's greatest wartime leaders.

rounds.clue: This Prime Minister once said, 'We are not here to do what is easy, but to do what is hard.'
rounds.tidbit: Ben Chifley was a train driver before entering politics, and he kept his union membership card in his wallet for the rest of his life.
rounds.explainer: Ben Chifley was Australia's 16th Prime Minister, serving from 1945 to 1949. A former railway engine driver, he was a passionate advocate for social justice and post-war reconstruction. His government introduced major initiatives like the Snowy Mountains Scheme and the national airline TAA. Chifley's famous 'light on the hill' speech about Labor's mission for social reform remains a cornerstone of Australian political rhetoric.

rounds.clue: This Prime Minister, who served three times, is often quoted as saying, 'Australia's destiny is to be the greatest nation in the world.'
rounds.tidbit: Andrew Fisher's government introduced Australia's first national currency, the Australian pound, replacing the British pound.
rounds.explainer: Andrew Fisher served as Australia's 5th Prime Minister across three non-consecutive terms between 1908 and 1915. A Scottish-born miner, he was a founding member of the Australian Labor Party. His government was known for its progressive reforms, including old-age pensions and maternity allowances. Fisher also committed Australia to support Britain in World War I, famously promising to help 'to the last man and the last shilling.'

rounds.clue: This Prime Minister was the first to represent a seat in Western Australia, and his government faced the Great Depression.
rounds.tidbit: James Scullin was the first Australian Prime Minister to serve without a majority in either house of Parliament.
rounds.explainer: James Scullin was Australia's 9th Prime Minister, serving from 1929 to 1932 during the Great Depression. He was a gifted orator and a staunch Catholic, which influenced his social views. His government struggled with economic crisis, leading to internal party splits and his eventual defeat. Despite his short tenure, Scullin's commitment to social welfare and national development left a lasting impact on the Labor Party.

rounds.clue: This Prime Minister was the world's first national leader from a labor party, taking office in 1904.
rounds.tidbit: Chris Watson was born in Chile to a British father and a New Zealand mother, making him the only Australian PM born overseas until 2022.
rounds.explainer: Chris Watson was Australia's 3rd Prime Minister, serving for just four months in 1904. He was the first national leader anywhere in the world to represent a labor party. Born in Valparaiso, Chile, he moved to Australia as a child and became a printer and unionist. His brief term set the precedent for Labor governments, and he later became a successful businessman and a key figure in the push for federation.

puzzles.background: This suburb's streets commemorate the pivotal battles and aircraft of World War II, from the deserts of North Africa to the jungles of the Pacific.
puzzles.reveal: It's Ashburton, where every street honors a WWII battle or aircraft.

rounds.clue: I was the site of the largest seaborne invasion in history, launched on June 6, 1944.
options: The Battle of the Coral Sea
rounds.tidbit: The Normandy invasion involved over 5,000 ships and 11,000 aircraft, the largest amphibious assault ever.
rounds.explainer: The Normandy Landings, codenamed Operation Overlord, were the Allied invasion of Nazi-occupied France on June 6, 1944. Over 156,000 troops landed on five beaches, suffering heavy casualties but establishing a crucial foothold in Western Europe. This operation marked the beginning of the end for Nazi Germany, leading to its surrender less than a year later. The success depended on elaborate deception plans and the largest naval armada ever assembled.

rounds.clue: This American fighter plane was nicknamed the 'Little Friend' by bomber crews because it protected them on long-range missions.
rounds.tidbit: The P-51 Mustang's range allowed it to escort bombers all the way to Berlin and back, a game-changer for the Allied air war.
rounds.explainer: The P-51 Mustang was a legendary American fighter aircraft that entered service in 1942. Its exceptional range and performance made it the ideal escort for heavy bombers, helping the Allies achieve air superiority over Europe. The Mustang was powered by a Rolls-Royce Merlin engine, which gave it incredible speed and agility. It was also used for ground attack and reconnaissance, becoming one of the most versatile and successful fighters of WWII.

rounds.clue: This flying boat was known as the 'Cat' and was famous for its ability to rescue downed airmen from the sea.
rounds.tidbit: Catalinas were nicknamed 'Dumbo' for their rescue missions, saving over 1,000 airmen in the Pacific alone.
rounds.explainer: The PBY Catalina was a versatile American flying boat used extensively in WWII for maritime patrol, anti-submarine warfare, and search-and-rescue. Its long range and ability to land on water made it invaluable for rescuing downed pilots and sailors. The Catalina served in every theater of the war, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and was also used by the Royal Australian Air Force. Its distinctive gull-wing design and durability earned it a legendary reputation.

rounds.clue: I was a port city in North Africa where Australian troops held out against German forces for eight months in 1941.
rounds.tidbit: The Australian 9th Division earned the nickname 'Rats of Tobruk' for their stubborn defense, which was a major morale boost for the Allies.
rounds.explainer: The Siege of Tobruk was a prolonged battle in Libya during the North African campaign of WWII. From April to December 1941, a garrison of Australian, British, Polish, and Czechoslovak troops held the strategically vital port against German and Italian forces led by General Erwin Rommel. The defenders' resilience and ingenuity, including using captured tanks and artillery, made Tobruk a symbol of Allied resistance. The siege was eventually lifted, but the Australian troops had already cemented their place in military history.

rounds.clue: This Australian-built aircraft was initially designed as a trainer, but it became a makeshift fighter and ground-attack plane in the Pacific.
rounds.tidbit: The Wirraway was the first all-metal aircraft designed and built in Australia, with over 750 produced during the war.
rounds.explainer: The CAC Wirraway was an Australian-designed and built aircraft that first flew in 1939. It was originally intended as a training aircraft, but after the outbreak of war in the Pacific, it was pressed into service as a combat aircraft. Wirraways flew ground-attack and reconnaissance missions, and even achieved a few aerial victories against Japanese aircraft. Despite being outclassed by modern fighters, the Wirraway was a crucial part of Australia's defense in the early years of WWII.

puzzles.background: This suburb's streets were named during a mid-20th-century housing boom, when developers looked to the night sky for inspiration. Every street here is named after a constellation, star, or planet.
puzzles.reveal: It was Balwyn North — where the streets are written in the stars.

rounds.clue: I am the brightest jewel of a summer triangle, the first star ever photographed, and the standard by which all other stars are measured.
rounds.tidbit: Vega was the first star ever photographed, in 1850, at Harvard College Observatory.
rounds.explainer: Vega is the brightest star in the constellation Lyra and the second-brightest in the northern night sky. It was the northern pole star around 12,000 BCE and will be again in about 13,700 years. As one of the most studied stars, it serves as the zero-point for the UBV photometric magnitude scale. Its rapid rotation gives it a distinctive oblate shape.

rounds.clue: I am the hunter with a belt of three stars, and my dog follows me across the winter sky.
rounds.tidbit: Orion contains two of the ten brightest stars in the sky: Rigel and Betelgeuse.
rounds.explainer: Orion is one of the most recognizable constellations in the night sky, visible from both hemispheres. In Greek mythology, Orion was a giant hunter who boasted he could kill any animal, leading to his death by a scorpion sent by Gaia. The constellation contains the Orion Nebula, a stellar nursery where new stars are born. Its three-star belt is a reliable guide for locating other bright stars.

rounds.clue: I am the planet with the rings, named for the Roman god of agriculture and time.
rounds.tidbit: Saturn's rings are so extensive they would span the distance from Earth to the Moon, yet they are only about 10 meters thick in places.
rounds.explainer: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun and the second-largest in the solar system, famous for its spectacular ring system made of ice and rock. It is a gas giant with a density lower than water, meaning it would float in a sufficiently large ocean. Its moon Titan has a thick atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane, making it a prime target for exploration. The planet's iconic rings were first observed by Galileo in 1610, though he mistook them for handles or moons.

rounds.clue: I am the bull that carried Europa across the sea, and my eye is a fiery red giant.
rounds.tidbit: Taurus contains the Crab Nebula, the remnant of a supernova observed in 1054 AD.
rounds.explainer: Taurus is a zodiac constellation representing the bull from Greek mythology, often associated with Zeus's disguise when he abducted Europa. Its brightest star, Aldebaran, is a red giant that marks the bull's eye. The constellation also hosts the Pleiades and Hyades star clusters, both visible to the naked eye. The Crab Nebula within Taurus is a pulsar wind nebula, a remnant of a stellar explosion that was so bright it was visible during the day.

rounds.clue: I am the bird with the hundred eyes, whose tail became the starry sky.
rounds.tidbit: Pavo contains one of the brightest globular clusters visible from the southern hemisphere, NGC 6752.
rounds.explainer: Pavo is a southern constellation introduced by Dutch navigators in the 16th century, named after the peacock. In Greek myth, the peacock was sacred to Hera, and its tail feathers bore the eyes of the giant Argus. The constellation is relatively faint but contains several notable deep-sky objects, including the globular cluster NGC 6752. Pavo is best viewed from latitudes south of the equator, making it a hidden gem for southern stargazers.

puzzles.background: Some Melbourne suburbs were developed during eras of national pride, with streets laid out to honour the country's political leaders. Here, every street is named after an Australian prime minister.
puzzles.reveal: It was Bentleigh East — where the streets pay tribute to the nation's prime ministers.

rounds.clue: I was Australia's second prime minister, serving three separate terms. I once said, 'We are a people who have come to stay.'
rounds.tidbit: Deakin was also a spiritualist who claimed to communicate with the dead through séances.
rounds.explainer: Alfred Deakin was a barrister, journalist, and politician who served as prime minister from 1903 to 1904, 1905 to 1908, and 1909 to 1910. He was a key figure in the federation movement and helped shape Australia's early national policies, including the White Australia policy and tariff protection. His eloquence earned him the nickname 'Affable Alfred.' He also founded the journal The Age's literary section and wrote under pseudonyms.

rounds.clue: I led Australia during the darkest days of World War II. My famous New Year's message in 1942 said, 'Australia looks to America, free of any pangs as to our traditional links or kinship with the United Kingdom.'
rounds.tidbit: Curtin was the first Australian prime minister to hold office from a seat in Western Australia.
rounds.explainer: John Curtin was Australia's 14th prime minister, serving from 1941 until his death in 1945. He took office just weeks before the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor and famously turned to the United States for protection, forging the ANZUS alliance. A former union official and journalist, he battled alcoholism and depression. His leadership during the war is widely regarded as one of Australia's finest.

rounds.clue: I was the 'Little Digger' who served as prime minister during World War I and later switched parties twice. I once declared, 'I am not a party man.'
rounds.tidbit: Hughes was the only prime minister to serve in both the House and Senate after switching chambers.
rounds.explainer: Billy Hughes was Australia's 7th prime minister, serving from 1915 to 1923. He was a fiery Welsh-born orator who led the country through World War I and fiercely advocated for conscription, which split the Labor Party and led him to form the Nationalist Party. He later helped found the United Australia Party and was a key figure at the Versailles Peace Conference, where he secured Australia's mandate over German New Guinea. He remained in parliament until his death in 1952, serving for over 50 years.

rounds.clue: I was the first Australian prime minister to die in office, and I once said, 'The welfare of the people is the supreme law.'
rounds.tidbit: Lyons was the only prime minister to have been a state premier before leading the nation.
rounds.explainer: Joseph Lyons was Australia's 10th prime minister, serving from 1932 to 1939. He began as a Labor premier of Tasmania but broke with the party over economic policy during the Great Depression and became the founding leader of the United Australia Party. His government implemented austerity measures and maintained close ties with Britain. He died of a heart attack in office, the first prime minister to do so.

rounds.clue: I was the prime minister who promised Australia would fight 'to the last man and the last shilling' in World War I. I also introduced the first national currency.
rounds.tidbit: Fisher's government established the Commonwealth Bank of Australia in 1911.
rounds.explainer: Andrew Fisher was Australia's 5th prime minister, serving three terms between 1908 and 1915. A Scottish-born miner and unionist, he led the Labor Party to victory in 1910, forming Australia's first federal majority government. His administration introduced old-age pensions, maternity allowances, and the national currency. His promise of support to Britain in 1914 was a defining moment of Australian history.

puzzles.background: In this leafy suburb, the streets pay tribute to the vibrant native flora of Australia. Each road is named after a beloved plant or tree that dots the landscape.
puzzles.reveal: It was Blackburn, where every street blooms with the names of native flora.

rounds.clue: I am the floral emblem of New South Wales, a striking red bloom that Aboriginal peoples used for nectar and timber. What am I?
rounds.tidbit: The waratah's name comes from the Eora Aboriginal word 'warada', meaning 'beautiful'.
rounds.explainer: The waratah (Telopea speciosissima) is a large shrub or small tree native to southeastern Australia, known for its brilliant crimson flower heads. It was first described by botanists in the 1790s and became the state emblem of New South Wales in 1962. The flower is a rich source of nectar for birds and insects, and its timber was historically used by Indigenous peoples for tools and weapons.

rounds.clue: Named in honor of a botanist who sailed with Captain Cook, my genus includes over 170 species. Which plant family am I?
rounds.tidbit: Banksias are also known as 'bottlebrushes' or 'honeysuckles' due to their dense flower spikes that attract nectar-feeding birds.
rounds.explainer: Banksias are a genus of evergreen trees and shrubs in the Proteaceae family, named after Sir Joseph Banks, the naturalist who accompanied Captain James Cook on the Endeavour voyage. They are renowned for their distinctive, cylindrical flower spikes that come in shades of yellow, orange, and red. Banksias are a vital food source for honeyeaters and other wildlife, and their woody seed pods are a classic feature of the Australian bush.

rounds.clue: I am Australia's national floral emblem, a golden bloom that symbolizes the country's spirit. Which plant am I?
rounds.tidbit: The golden wattle (Acacia pycnantha) became Australia's official floral emblem in 1988, and its green and gold colors are featured on the national coat of arms.
rounds.explainer: Acacias, commonly known as wattles, are a diverse genus of shrubs and trees with over 1,000 species in Australia alone. The golden wattle, with its bright yellow pom-pom flowers, is celebrated on National Wattle Day each September. Acacias are nitrogen-fixing plants that improve soil fertility, and their wood is used for furniture, tools, and tannin production. The iconic silhouette of the wattle is a symbol of resilience and unity in Australian culture.

rounds.clue: I am a genus of shrubs and trees known for my papery bark and aromatic leaves, often found in wetlands. What am I?
rounds.tidbit: The tea tree oil, widely used for its antiseptic properties, is extracted from the leaves of Melaleuca alternifolia.
rounds.explainer: Melaleucas, also called paperbarks or honey myrtles, belong to the myrtle family and thrive in damp, swampy areas. Their distinctive peeling bark protects them from fire and helps them survive in harsh conditions. Tea tree oil, derived from several species, has been used for centuries by Indigenous Australians for medicinal purposes and is now a global natural remedy. These hardy plants also provide essential habitat for birds and insects in wetland ecosystems.

rounds.clue: My genus includes over 140 species, many with spiky leaves and unique woody fruits. Which plant am I?
rounds.tidbit: Hakea fruits are so hard that they often need fire to open and release seeds, ensuring the next generation thrives after a bushfire.
rounds.explainer: Hakeas are a genus of flowering plants in the Proteaceae family, named after German botanist Baron Christian Ludwig von Hake. They are known for their tough, often needle-like leaves and clusters of small, intricate flowers that attract birds and insects. The woody seed pods, called follicles, can remain closed for years, opening only after a fire or when the plant dies. Hakeas are a striking and resilient addition to the Australian landscape, with many species used in horticulture.

puzzles.background: In Melbourne's western suburbs, a post-war estate took to the skies with streets honouring the pioneers and machines of flight. Every street here is named after aviation legends, airlines, or the aircraft that shaped aerial history.
puzzles.reveal: It was Braybrook — where the streets soar with aviation heritage.

rounds.clue: I crossed an ocean in a Fokker, then vanished over the Bay of Bengal in 1935. Who am I?
rounds.tidbit: His Fokker was named the 'Southern Cross', and he was the first to fly across the Pacific from the US to Australia.
rounds.explainer: Sir Charles Kingsford Smith, often called 'Smithy', was a pioneering Australian aviator who completed the first transpacific flight in 1928. He set numerous long-distance records and became a national hero. His disappearance in 1935 remains one of aviation's enduring mysteries. He was knighted for his contributions to flight.

rounds.clue: I flew solo from England to Australia in 1928, and my name now graces a Queensland town and a wartime aircraft. Who was I?
rounds.tidbit: He was known as 'Hustling Hinkler' and completed the first solo flight from England to Australia in a de Havilland DH.60 Moth.
rounds.explainer: Bert Hinkler was a Queensland-born aviator and inventor who set multiple long-distance flying records. His 1928 solo flight from England to Australia cut the previous time in half, making him an international sensation. He later died in a crash in Italy in 1933. The town of Hinkler in Queensland and the Hinkler aircraft are named in his honour.

rounds.clue: I am a two-seat trainer that became a makeshift fighter in the Pacific, built by the Commonwealth Aircraft Corporation. What am I?
rounds.tidbit: The Wirraway was based on the North American NA-16, and its name comes from an Aboriginal word meaning 'challenge'.
rounds.explainer: The CAC Wirraway was an Australian-designed and built training and general-purpose aircraft used during World War II. It was derived from the North American NA-16 and served as a dive bomber and fighter in emergencies. The aircraft was a crucial step in establishing Australia's domestic aviation industry. Over 750 were produced between 1939 and 1946.

rounds.clue: My name means 'young eagle' in an Aboriginal language, and I was a basic trainer that served the RAAF for over two decades. What am I?
rounds.tidbit: The Winjeel was designed specifically for the RAAF's pilot training program and featured a distinctive 'spatted' undercarriage.
rounds.explainer: The CAC Winjeel was an Australian basic trainer that entered service in 1955 and remained active until the late 1970s. Its name, meaning 'young eagle', reflects its role in training fledgling pilots. The aircraft was known for its robust design and forgiving handling. It was replaced by the Pilatus PC-9 in the 1980s.

rounds.clue: I was a heavy bomber that flew from Australia to strike Japanese targets, and my name echoes freedom. What aircraft am I?
rounds.tidbit: The B-24 was the most produced American military aircraft of WWII, with over 18,000 built.
rounds.explainer: The Consolidated B-24 Liberator was a four-engine heavy bomber used extensively by Allied forces in World War II. It served in the Pacific, Europe, and the Mediterranean, including with the Royal Australian Air Force. Its long range made it ideal for maritime patrol and bombing missions. The aircraft's distinctive high-mounted wing and twin tail made it easily recognisable.

puzzles.background: In this suburb, the streets evoke the rolling countryside and historic towns of Britain, with names borrowed from English counties, villages, and rivers.
puzzles.reveal: It was Bundoora — where every street is a nod to British towns and rivers.

rounds.clue: This river flows through a city famous for its music scene in the 1960s, and its name is often linked to the Beatles.
rounds.tidbit: The Mersey is only 70 miles long, but it's one of the most famous rivers in pop culture thanks to Gerry and the Pacemakers' 'Ferry Cross the Mersey'.
rounds.explainer: The River Mersey flows through Liverpool and Manchester in northwest England. It's been a vital trade route since the Industrial Revolution, but it's best known today as the river that inspired the Beatles' song 'Mersey Beat' and the 1965 film 'Ferry Cross the Mersey'. The river's name comes from the Old English 'Mǽres ēa', meaning 'boundary river', as it once marked the border between the kingdoms of Mercia and Northumbria.

rounds.clue: This eastern English county is home to the city of Norwich and the famous Broads, a network of navigable rivers and lakes.
rounds.tidbit: Norfolk is home to the largest seal colony in England, with more than 3,000 grey seals at Blakeney Point.
rounds.explainer: Norfolk is a county in East Anglia, known for its flat landscapes, medieval churches, and the Norfolk Broads. It was a major center of the wool trade in the Middle Ages, and its capital, Norwich, was once one of England's largest cities. The county's name derives from the 'North Folk' of the Angles, who settled there in the 5th century. Norfolk also has a rich maritime history, with ports like Great Yarmouth playing a key role in fishing and trade.

rounds.clue: This historic county on England's south coast is known for its chalk cliffs and was once a kingdom of the South Saxons.
rounds.tidbit: Sussex is the only English county with its own national anthem, 'Sussex by the Sea', which was popular with soldiers in World War I.
rounds.explainer: Sussex is a historic county in southeast England, famous for the white cliffs of Dover (though those are actually in Kent) and the rolling South Downs. It was one of the seven kingdoms of Anglo-Saxon England, founded by the South Saxons in the 5th century. The county has a long tradition of ironworking and shipbuilding, and its coastline was a frontline during the Battle of Britain. Today, Sussex is known for its scenic countryside, historic castles like Arundel, and the seaside city of Brighton.

rounds.clue: This district in south London is named after the 'north wood' of the Great North Wood, an ancient oak forest.
rounds.tidbit: The Great North Wood once stretched for seven miles and was a favorite haunt of the 17th-century diarist Samuel Pepys.
rounds.explainer: Norwood is a district in the London Borough of Croydon, whose name comes from the 'North Wood' of the Great North Wood, a vast area of oak trees that covered much of south London. The wood was a source of timber for shipbuilding and charcoal for the city's industries. In the 19th century, Norwood became a desirable residential area, and it was home to the Crystal Palace after it was moved from Hyde Park in 1854. Today, Norwood retains some of its green spaces, including the Norwood Grove and the South Norwood Country Park.

rounds.clue: This market town in Surrey is known for its castle and was once a residence of the Bishops of Winchester.
rounds.tidbit: Farnham's castle was built in the 12th century and was used as a prison during the English Civil War.
rounds.explainer: Farnham is a historic market town in Surrey, England, located at the northern edge of the South Downs. It has been a settlement since Roman times, and its name comes from the Old English 'Fearnham', meaning 'homestead where ferns grow'. The town's most prominent landmark is Farnham Castle, which served as the palace of the Bishops of Winchester for over 800 years. Farnham was also a center of the hop-growing industry, which supplied beer brewers across Britain, and it retains a charming Georgian high street.

puzzles.background: In this northern suburb, the streets form a literary constellation, each one named after a celebrated poet or writer whose words have shaped the English language.
puzzles.reveal: It was Bundoora, where the streets pay homage to the great poets of the literary canon.

rounds.clue: This playwright and poet from Stratford-upon-Avon is often called the Bard of Avon. His works include 'Hamlet' and 'Romeo and Juliet'.
rounds.tidbit: Shakespeare invented over 1,700 words, including 'bedazzled' and 'swagger'.
rounds.explainer: William Shakespeare (1564-1616) is widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language. His 39 plays and 154 sonnets have been translated into every major language and performed more often than those of any other playwright. He was a co-owner of the Globe Theatre in London, and his influence on literature and theater is immeasurable.

rounds.clue: This Romantic poet found his muse in the Lake District and wrote 'I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud'. He was once Britain's Poet Laureate.
rounds.tidbit: Wordsworth's poem 'I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud' was inspired by a walk he took with his sister Dorothy in 1802.
rounds.explainer: William Wordsworth (1770-1850) was a central figure of the English Romantic movement. His 'Lyrical Ballads', co-written with Samuel Taylor Coleridge, marked a turning point in English poetry. He served as Poet Laureate from 1843 until his death, and his deep connection to nature is celebrated in works like 'The Prelude'.

rounds.clue: This Romantic poet wrote 'Ozymandias' and 'Ode to the West Wind'. He drowned at age 29 off the coast of Italy.
rounds.tidbit: Shelley's heart was reportedly snatched from his funeral pyre by his friend Edward Trelawny and kept as a keepsake.
rounds.explainer: Percy Bysshe Shelley (1792-1822) was a radical and visionary poet of the Romantic era. His works, including 'Prometheus Unbound' and 'Adonais', are known for their lyrical beauty and political passion. An outspoken atheist and advocate for free love, he was expelled from Oxford for publishing a pamphlet on atheism.

rounds.clue: This American poet famously wrote 'The Road Not Taken' and 'Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening'. He was a four-time Pulitzer Prize winner.
rounds.tidbit: Frost's poem 'The Road Not Taken' is often misread as a celebration of individualism, but it is actually a gentle mockery of self-importance.
rounds.explainer: Robert Frost (1874-1963) is one of the most beloved American poets of the 20th century. Though born in San Francisco, he became synonymous with New England's landscapes. He recited his poem 'The Gift Outright' at John F. Kennedy's inauguration in 1961, and his work often explores themes of rural life and human isolation.

rounds.clue: This British author wrote 'The Jungle Book' and 'If—'. He was the first English-language writer to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature.
rounds.tidbit: Kipling's 'If—' was voted Britain's favorite poem in 1995.
rounds.explainer: Rudyard Kipling (1865-1936) was born in India and became a chronicler of the British Empire. His works, including 'Kim' and 'The Man Who Would Be King', are celebrated for their vivid storytelling. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1907, the youngest recipient at the time, and his influence on adventure fiction is profound.

puzzles.background: In this northern suburb, the streets honor the nation's leaders, each one a tribute to the men who shaped Australia's political landscape.
puzzles.reveal: It was Bundoora, where every street is named after an Australian prime minister.

rounds.clue: The 'Pig Iron Bob' who led Australia through the early Cold War and was its longest-serving prime minister.
rounds.tidbit: Menzies once said, 'I did my best' when asked about his legacy.
rounds.explainer: Robert Menzies served two non-consecutive terms as prime minister, totaling over 18 years, the longest in Australian history. He founded the Liberal Party in 1944 and was a key figure in the Cold War, aligning Australia with the United States. His famous 'Forgotten People' speech in 1942 outlined his vision for the middle class. Menzies also knighted himself in 1963, a move that drew much criticism.

rounds.clue: The wartime leader who famously declared, 'We shall hold this country as a citadel' during the darkest days of WWII.
rounds.tidbit: Curtin was the first prime minister to have no university education.
rounds.explainer: John Curtin was Australia's 14th prime minister, serving from 1941 to 1945 during World War II. He famously turned to the United States for protection, stating that Australia looked to America 'free of any pangs as to our traditional links of kinship with the United Kingdom.' His leadership was marked by a deep sense of duty and sacrifice, and he died in office in 1945. He remains one of Australia's most revered leaders.

rounds.clue: The prime minister who disappeared while swimming at Cheviot Beach in 1967, leaving the nation in shock.
rounds.tidbit: Holt was the first Australian prime minister to have a US Navy vessel named after him.
rounds.explainer: Harold Holt served as prime minister from 1966 until his mysterious disappearance in December 1967. He was an enthusiastic swimmer and was known for his energetic style. His disappearance sparked numerous conspiracy theories, but no body was ever found. He was a strong supporter of the US alliance and increased Australian troop commitments in Vietnam.

rounds.clue: The fiery 'Little Digger' who was prime minister during World War I and played a key role at the Versailles Peace Conference.
rounds.tidbit: Hughes was the only prime minister to have been born outside Australia (in London).
rounds.explainer: Billy Hughes was a fiery and controversial figure who served as prime minister from 1915 to 1923. He was a passionate advocate for conscription during WWI, which split the Labor Party and led to his expulsion. At the Versailles Peace Conference, he famously fought for Australian interests and reparations from Germany. He was the last surviving member of the British Cabinet to have served in WWI.

rounds.clue: Australia's first prime minister, who famously said, 'For the first time in history, we have a nation for a continent, and a continent for a nation.'
rounds.tidbit: Barton was a champion tennis player in his youth.
rounds.explainer: Edmund Barton was Australia's first prime minister, serving from 1901 to 1903. He was a key figure in the federation movement and was known for his eloquence and legal mind. After leaving politics, he became a founding justice of the High Court of Australia. His legacy is indelibly linked to the birth of the Australian nation.

puzzles.background: In this leafy eastern suburb, the streets pay homage to the country's unique plant life—each one a tribute to the native flora that defines the landscape.
puzzles.reveal: It was Burwood, where the streets bloom with native flora!

rounds.clue: Named after a genus of over 170 species, this plant was among the first to be scientifically described by an English botanist during Captain Cook's 1770 voyage.
rounds.tidbit: Banksias have been around for millions of years, with fossilized leaves found in 50-million-year-old deposits.
rounds.explainer: The genus Banksia was named in honor of Sir Joseph Banks, the naturalist who accompanied Captain Cook on the HMS Endeavour. These striking plants are famous for their distinctive, brush-like flower spikes that attract a variety of nectar-feeding birds and insects. With over 170 species, they range from groundcovers to tall trees, many of which are fire-adapted and release seeds only after a blaze.

rounds.clue: The floral emblem of New South Wales, this striking red flower is known for its large, showy heads that bloom in spring.
rounds.tidbit: The waratah is so beloved that it's protected by law in New South Wales, making it illegal to pick without a license.
rounds.explainer: The waratah is a member of the Proteaceae family and is renowned for its vivid crimson flower heads, which are actually clusters of up to 250 individual flowers. It has been a cultural icon for centuries, used by Indigenous Australians for nectar and as a symbol of resilience. Today, it's a popular cut flower and a proud emblem of the state, celebrated in festivals and gardens alike.

rounds.clue: This name covers over a thousand species, including the golden wattle, which appears on a national coat of arms.
rounds.tidbit: Australia's national floral emblem, the golden wattle, is a type of this plant and blooms on September 1, National Wattle Day.
rounds.explainer: Acacia is the largest genus of flowering plants in Australia, with over 1,000 species, from shrubs to tall trees. They are known for their fluffy, ball-shaped or elongated clusters of tiny flowers, often yellow or cream, and their feathery or leathery leaves. Acacias are vital to ecosystems, fixing nitrogen in the soil and providing food and shelter for wildlife. The golden wattle (Acacia pycnantha) has been a symbol of unity and resilience since 1988, featured on the Australian coat of arms.

rounds.clue: This plant's oil is a household remedy, famed for its antiseptic properties, and its leaves were used by Indigenous Australians for healing.
rounds.tidbit: The name 'tea tree' was coined by Captain Cook's crew, who brewed the leaves into a fragrant tea to prevent scurvy.
rounds.explainer: Tea tree, specifically Melaleuca alternifolia, is a small tree native to the northeast coast of New South Wales. Its leaves are the source of tea tree oil, a powerful natural antiseptic that has been used for centuries by Indigenous Australians to treat wounds and infections. The oil gained global popularity after World War II when it became a standard medical supply for soldiers. Today, tea tree oil is a staple in natural health products, from skincare to cleaning agents.

rounds.clue: This name is shared by a national emblem and a type of tree that blooms into golden, fluffy balls every spring.
rounds.tidbit: Australia's national colors, green and gold, were officially adopted in 1984, inspired by the leaves and flowers of this plant.
rounds.explainer: Wattle is the common name for many acacia species, particularly the golden wattle, which is Australia's national floral emblem. The name 'wattle' comes from the Old English word for a flexible twig, as early settlers used the branches for building fences and walls. Wattles are incredibly diverse, with species ranging from small shrubs to tall trees, and their bright yellow blooms are a beloved sign of spring. They also play a crucial role in the landscape, helping to stabilize soil and support native wildlife.

puzzles.background: In this leafy suburb, the streets pay homage to the great wordsmiths of English literature, from the Romantic era to the Victorian age.
puzzles.reveal: It was Canterbury, where every street is a tribute to a literary legend.

rounds.clue: I awoke one morning and found myself famous. Who am I?
rounds.tidbit: Lord Byron was known for his scandalous love affairs and once kept a pet bear while at Cambridge University.
rounds.explainer: Lord Byron (1788–1824) was a leading figure of the Romantic movement, known for his flamboyant lifestyle and works like 'Don Juan' and 'Childe Harold's Pilgrimage.' He famously said he awoke to find himself famous after the publication of the latter. Byron's life was marked by debt, scandalous affairs, and a heroic death while fighting for Greek independence. His poetry and persona made him a celebrity in his own time, and his influence on literature and culture endures today.

rounds.clue: I wrote the Waverley novels but kept my identity a secret for years. Who am I?
rounds.tidbit: Sir Walter Scott is often credited with popularizing the historical novel with works like 'Ivanhoe' and 'Rob Roy.'
rounds.explainer: Sir Walter Scott (1771–1832) was a Scottish historical novelist, poet, and historian, celebrated for classics like 'Ivanhoe' and 'Rob Roy.' He published the Waverley novels anonymously, and the mystery of their authorship only added to his fame. Scott was a key figure in the Romantic movement and helped shape the modern historical novel. His legacy includes not only his literary works but also the revival of Scottish cultural identity.

rounds.clue: I wrote an epic about the fall of man, and I was blind when I composed it. Who am I?
rounds.tidbit: John Milton dictated 'Paradise Lost' to his daughters after going completely blind.
rounds.explainer: John Milton (1608–1674) was a 17th-century English poet best known for the epic poem 'Paradise Lost,' which explores the biblical story of the fall of man. Despite going blind in his forties, he composed the poem and dictated it to helpers. Milton was also a passionate political writer, serving as a civil servant under Oliver Cromwell. His work has had a profound influence on English literature and the English language itself.

rounds.clue: I was the first to be named Poet Laureate of England. Who am I?
rounds.tidbit: John Dryden was appointed the first official Poet Laureate by King Charles II in 1668.
rounds.explainer: John Dryden (1631–1700) was an influential English poet, literary critic, and playwright who dominated the literary scene of the Restoration era. He was appointed the first Poet Laureate in 1668, a role he held for two decades. Dryden's works include the satirical poem 'Absalom and Achitophel' and the play 'All for Love.' His writing marked a transition from the metaphysical poets to the Age of Reason, and his use of heroic couplets influenced many later poets.

rounds.clue: I wrote 'Ode to a Nightingale' and died young in Rome. Who am I?
rounds.tidbit: John Keats died of tuberculosis at the age of 25, and his last request was to be buried under a tombstone reading 'Here lies one whose name was writ in water.'
rounds.explainer: John Keats (1795–1821) was a second-generation Romantic poet whose works, including 'Ode to a Nightingale' and 'To Autumn,' are celebrated for their rich imagery and sensuous language. Despite a short life plagued by illness and financial hardship, he produced a remarkable body of poetry. Keats's letters and poems reveal his deep thoughts on beauty, mortality, and art. He died in Rome at 25, and his legacy has grown to place him among the most beloved English poets.

puzzles.background: This leafy suburb's streets commemorate the battles, wars, and campaigns of the 19th century, particularly the Crimean War and other conflicts of the British Empire.
puzzles.reveal: It was Caulfield North — where every street is a battle cry.

rounds.clue: This battle gave its name to a knitted garment worn by soldiers to keep warm, and to a famous ill-fated cavalry charge.
options: The Charge of the Light Brigade
rounds.tidbit: The famous 'Charge of the Light Brigade' happened during this battle, immortalized in Tennyson's poem.
rounds.explainer: The Battle of Balaclava, fought on October 25, 1854, was part of the Siege of Sevastopol in the Crimean War. It saw the British and French against the Russian Empire, and included the disastrous Charge of the Light Brigade, where about 600 cavalrymen charged into heavy Russian artillery fire. The battle also gave the world the 'balaclava' — a woolen head covering worn by soldiers to protect against the cold.

rounds.clue: This battle was nicknamed 'the Soldier's Battle' because the fog was so thick that officers lost control and soldiers fought in small groups.
rounds.tidbit: Fought in dense fog, the Battle of Inkerman was so chaotic that it was called 'the Soldier's Battle'.
rounds.explainer: The Battle of Inkerman, fought on November 5, 1854, was a key engagement of the Crimean War. British and French forces repelled a Russian attack on their positions, despite being outnumbered. The thick fog made command nearly impossible, leading to small-unit actions and hand-to-hand combat. It was a costly victory, with heavy casualties on both sides, and helped maintain the siege of Sevastopol.

rounds.clue: The first major battle of the Crimean War, fought on a river, and the name of a famous flower that grew from the blood of soldiers.
rounds.tidbit: The Alma flower, a deep red variety, is said to have sprung from the blood of soldiers who fell in this battle.
rounds.explainer: The Battle of Alma, fought on September 20, 1854, was the first major engagement of the Crimean War. Allied British, French, and Ottoman forces defeated the Russian army on the banks of the Alma River. It was a significant victory that opened the way to Sevastopol. A legend grew that a red flower, the 'Alma flower', bloomed from the blood of the fallen, and it became a symbol of remembrance.

rounds.clue: This was a massive earthen fortification that became the key to a city's defense, and its fall led to the end of a long siege.
rounds.tidbit: The Malakoff Redoubt was a massive earthwork fortress that the French finally captured in September 1855, leading to the fall of Sevastopol.
rounds.explainer: The Malakoff Redoubt was a key defensive position overlooking Sevastopol during the Crimean War. It was a massive earthwork fortification that the Russians had heavily armed. After months of siege, French forces stormed it on September 8, 1855, and its capture forced the Russians to abandon the city. The name 'Malakoff' became famous in France, and many streets and squares across the world bear its name.

rounds.clue: This British officer's name is forever linked to a sleeve style on coats, and he commanded allied forces in the Crimean War.
rounds.tidbit: Lord Raglan gave his name to the 'raglan sleeve', a coat design that allows for easier arm movement.
rounds.explainer: Lord Raglan, born FitzRoy Somerset, was a British army officer who served as commander-in-chief of British forces during the Crimean War. He had lost his right arm at the Battle of Waterloo, which inspired the design of the raglan sleeve. He led the British army at the battles of Alma, Balaclava, and Inkerman, and died in 1855 during the siege of Sevastopol. His name lives on in fashion and in this street.

puzzles.background: In this Melbourne suburb, the streets are named after celestial bodies and space concepts, reflecting a fascination with the cosmos.
puzzles.reveal: It was Caulfield South — where every street is a star or planet.

rounds.clue: I am the largest planet in the solar system, with a storm that has raged for centuries. Which planet am I?
rounds.tidbit: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm larger than Earth that has been observed for over 350 years.
rounds.explainer: Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and the largest in the solar system, with a mass more than twice that of all other planets combined. It is a gas giant with no solid surface, composed mostly of hydrogen and helium. Its iconic Great Red Spot is a persistent anticyclonic storm. Jupiter has 95 known moons, including four large Galilean moons discovered by Galileo in 1610.

rounds.clue: I am known for my magnificent rings, made of ice and rock. Which planet am I?
rounds.tidbit: Saturn's rings are so vast they could fit Earth's diameter 8 times, yet they are only about 10 meters thick in places.
rounds.explainer: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun, a gas giant with a distinctive ring system composed of countless particles ranging from micrometers to meters in size. The rings are made mostly of water ice, with some rocky debris and dust. Saturn is less dense than water, so it would float in a sufficiently large ocean. Its moon Titan has a thick atmosphere and liquid methane lakes, making it a prime target for exploration.

rounds.clue: I am the Red Planet, named after the Roman god of war. Which planet am I?
rounds.tidbit: Mars is home to Olympus Mons, the tallest volcano in the solar system, nearly three times the height of Mount Everest.
rounds.explainer: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun, a cold desert world with a thin atmosphere of mostly carbon dioxide. Its reddish appearance comes from iron oxide (rust) on its surface. Mars has polar ice caps, seasonal dust storms, and evidence of ancient riverbeds and lakes, suggesting it once had liquid water. Numerous rovers and orbiters, including NASA's Perseverance, are currently studying the planet to search for signs of past life and prepare for human exploration.

rounds.clue: I am the hottest planet in the solar system, with a thick toxic atmosphere. Which planet am I?
rounds.tidbit: Venus spins backwards compared to most planets, meaning the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east.
rounds.explainer: Venus is the second planet from the Sun and the hottest, with surface temperatures around 465°C (870°F) due to a runaway greenhouse effect from its dense CO2 atmosphere. It is often called Earth's 'sister planet' due to similar size and composition, but its surface is hidden by thick clouds of sulfuric acid. Venus has the longest day of any planet, lasting 243 Earth days, and its rotation is retrograde. It was the first planet visited by a spacecraft (Mariner 2) and is often called the 'Morning Star' or 'Evening Star' when visible from Earth.

rounds.clue: I am the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun, with extreme temperature swings. Which planet am I?
rounds.tidbit: A year on Mercury is just 88 Earth days, but a single day-night cycle lasts 176 Earth days.
rounds.explainer: Mercury is the smallest planet in our solar system and the closest to the Sun, orbiting at an average distance of just 58 million kilometers. It has no atmosphere to retain heat, so temperatures can swing from -180°C at night to 430°C during the day. Mercury's surface is heavily cratered, resembling our Moon. Despite its proximity to the Sun, it is not the hottest planet (Venus is) because its thin exosphere cannot trap heat. The planet was named after the swift Roman messenger god, fitting its fast orbit.

puzzles.background: In this northern suburb, the streets pay homage to the art and science of capturing light, from the earliest cameras to modern digital photography.
puzzles.reveal: It was Coburg North — where every street is a snapshot of photographic history!

rounds.clue: This word for a curved piece of glass comes from the Latin for 'lentil', because of its shape.
rounds.tidbit: The first camera lens was a simple pinhole, and it wasn't until the 16th century that glass lenses were added to improve clarity.
rounds.explainer: The lens is the eye of the camera, focusing light to create a sharp image. Its name derives from the Latin 'lens' for lentil, which the convex shape resembles. Early cameras used a pinhole, but by the 1800s, glass lenses allowed for faster exposures and finer detail. Today, lenses come in countless varieties, from wide-angle to telephoto, each bending light in unique ways.

rounds.clue: This opening controls how much light enters the camera; its size is measured in f-stops, and a smaller number means a larger opening.
rounds.tidbit: The word 'aperture' comes from the Latin 'apertura', meaning 'an opening'.
rounds.explainer: The aperture is the adjustable opening in a camera lens that regulates the amount of light reaching the sensor or film. It also affects depth of field—a wide aperture blurs the background, while a narrow one keeps everything in focus. The f-stop scale, like f/2.8 or f/16, is a ratio of the lens's focal length to the diameter of the opening. This simple mechanism is key to both exposure and creative control in photography.

rounds.clue: This term, meaning the sharpness of an image, comes from the Latin for 'hearth' or 'fireplace'—where the home's center was.
rounds.tidbit: In ancient Rome, the focus was the central hearth of a house, and later came to mean the center of activity—and eventually the point where light rays converge.
rounds.explainer: In optics, focus is the point where light rays converge to form a sharp image. The term evolved from the Latin 'focus' meaning 'hearth', as the fireplace was the focal point of a Roman home. In photography, achieving focus is essential for a clear picture; modern autofocus systems use sensors and algorithms to adjust the lens instantly. The concept of focus also extends metaphorically to attention and concentration.

rounds.clue: This tiny unit of a digital image is a portmanteau of 'picture' and 'element'.
rounds.tidbit: The first digital image ever scanned used a resolution of 176×176 pixels—a square about the size of a postage stamp.
rounds.explainer: A pixel is the smallest controllable element of a digital image, a square of color that combines with millions of others to form a picture. The term was coined in the 1960s from 'picture element'. The number of pixels, often measured in megapixels, determines a camera's resolution. The first digital image, created by Russell Kirsch in 1957, was just 176×176 pixels, a far cry from today's multi-megapixel sensors.

rounds.clue: This term for a quick photograph comes from a hunting phrase meaning a hurried shot taken without careful aim.
rounds.tidbit: The word 'snapshot' was first used in the 1800s by hunters to describe a quick, instinctive shot, and was later adopted by photographers.
rounds.explainer: A snapshot is a photograph taken quickly, often informally, without elaborate preparation. The term originated in the 19th century among sportsmen to describe a hurried gunshot. By the late 1800s, with the advent of portable cameras like the Kodak, it became synonymous with casual photography. Snapshots capture spontaneous moments, making them treasured records of everyday life.

puzzles.background: This waterfront district was built around a working harbour, and its streets honour the ships, explorers, and maritime milestones that shaped Australia's southern coast.
puzzles.reveal: It was Docklands — where every street tells a tale of the sea.

rounds.clue: I was a topsail schooner that carried the first settlers to their new home on the Yarra in 1835. My name is often misspelled with an 's' instead of a 'z'.
rounds.tidbit: The original Enterprize was only 54 feet long and carried 10 passengers, 2 crew, and a few sheep on its historic voyage.
rounds.explainer: The Enterprize was a small topsail schooner that sailed from Launceston to Port Phillip Bay in 1835, carrying the party that founded the settlement that would become Melbourne. Its name is often cited as 'Enterprise', but the vessel's official name used the 'z'. A replica of the ship now sails as a tourist attraction on the Yarra River. The voyage marked the beginning of permanent European settlement in the area.

rounds.clue: I was the first European to sail through the strait that now bears my name, proving that Van Diemen's Land was an island. I was a naval surgeon by trade.
rounds.tidbit: George Bass once survived a 600-mile journey in a whaleboat with just four companions, mapping the coast as he went.
rounds.explainer: George Bass was a British naval surgeon and explorer who, with Matthew Flinders, circumnavigated Van Diemen's Land in 1798–99. He earlier charted the coast near Sydney in a small open boat, earning a reputation for daring. The strait between mainland Australia and Tasmania was named in his honour. He disappeared in 1803 while on a voyage to South America, and his fate remains unknown.

rounds.clue: In 1802, my ship met a French expedition near the mouth of the Murray River — a peaceful meeting that gave this coastline its name. I was the British commander.
rounds.tidbit: Matthew Flinders was the first person to circumnavigate Australia and is credited with naming the continent 'Australia'.
rounds.explainer: Matthew Flinders was a British navigator and cartographer who led the first circumnavigation of Australia from 1801 to 1803. His encounter with Nicolas Baudin's French expedition at Encounter Bay was a famous moment of international scientific courtesy. Flinders' charts were so accurate that many were still in use a century later. He also wrote 'A Voyage to Terra Australis' while imprisoned by the French on Mauritius.

rounds.clue: I commanded the French expedition that mapped the southern coast of Australia, and my meeting with a British rival was remarkably cordial. My name is often mispronounced 'Baw-din'.
rounds.tidbit: Despite being rivals, Nicolas Baudin and Matthew Flinders exchanged charts and supplies during their famous meeting in 1802.
rounds.explainer: Nicolas Baudin led the French scientific expedition of 1800–1804, which charted much of the Australian coastline with remarkable precision. His ships, Géographe and Naturaliste, carried a team of naturalists who collected thousands of specimens. His meeting with Flinders at Encounter Bay was a model of peaceful cooperation between warring nations. Baudin died in Mauritius on the return voyage, and many of his findings were published posthumously.

rounds.clue: I was a tiny boat, just 8 feet long, that carried two famous explorers on a daring coastal survey. My name suggests a fairy-tale character.
rounds.tidbit: The Tom Thumb was so small that its crew had to sit still to avoid capsizing, yet it completed several perilous journeys.
rounds.explainer: The Tom Thumb was a diminutive open boat used by George Bass and Matthew Flinders in 1796 to explore the coast south of Sydney. Despite its size, it survived rough seas and even an encounter with Indigenous Australians. The voyages proved the explorers' skill and helped launch their later careers. The boat's name has become a symbol of audacious seamanship.

puzzles.background: In this Melbourne suburb, the streets pay homage to the greats of English literature, from poets to novelists. Each street name is a tribute to a famous writer.
puzzles.reveal: It was Elwood — where every street is a literary legend.

rounds.clue: I was described as 'mad, bad, and dangerous to know' by Lady Caroline Lamb. My epic poem 'Don Juan' remains unfinished.
rounds.tidbit: Lord Byron kept a pet bear while at Cambridge, as college rules forbade dogs.
rounds.explainer: George Gordon, Lord Byron, was a leading figure in the Romantic movement, known for his flamboyant lifestyle and passionate poetry. His works, including 'Childe Harold's Pilgrimage' and 'Don Juan', captured the imagination of Europe. He died of fever in Missolonghi, Greece, while supporting their fight for independence, and is considered a Greek national hero.

rounds.clue: I was the Poet Laureate of the United Kingdom for over four decades, and wrote 'The Charge of the Light Brigade'.
rounds.tidbit: Tennyson's 'In Memoriam A.H.H.' was a favorite of Queen Victoria, who found comfort in it after Prince Albert's death.
rounds.explainer: Alfred, Lord Tennyson was the most popular poet of the Victorian era, known for works like 'Ulysses' and 'The Lady of Shalott'. His poetry often explored themes of mortality, nature, and mythology. He served as Poet Laureate from 1850 until his death in 1892, making him the longest-serving laureate to that point.

rounds.clue: I wrote 'Ozymandias' and 'Ode to the West Wind', and I drowned in Italy at the age of 29.
rounds.tidbit: After Shelley's death, his heart was reportedly saved from the funeral pyre and given to his wife Mary.
rounds.explainer: Percy Bysshe Shelley was a radical and visionary poet of the Romantic era, celebrated for his lyrical verse and political idealism. His works include 'Prometheus Unbound' and 'Adonais', an elegy for his friend John Keats. He drowned in a storm while sailing in the Gulf of Spezia, and his body was cremated on the beach.

rounds.clue: I wrote about the struggles of Victorian London, and my characters include Oliver Twist and Ebenezer Scrooge.
rounds.tidbit: Dickens wrote 'A Christmas Carol' in just six weeks, and it was published in 1843.
rounds.explainer: Charles Dickens was a prolific novelist of the Victorian era, known for his vivid characters and social commentary. His novels, including 'David Copperfield' and 'Great Expectations', were serialized in magazines and hugely popular. He also gave public readings of his works, which drew large audiences on both sides of the Atlantic.

rounds.clue: I am Scotland's national poet, and my song 'Auld Lang Syne' is sung on New Year's Eve worldwide.
rounds.tidbit: Robert Burns was a farmer who wrote over 550 poems and songs, many in the Scots dialect.
rounds.explainer: Robert Burns, also known as Rabbie Burns, is celebrated as the national poet of Scotland. His works, such as 'A Red, Red Rose' and 'Tam o' Shanter', are beloved for their wit and emotional depth. He was also a pioneer of the Romantic movement, and his birthday, January 25, is celebrated with Burns Night suppers.

puzzles.background: This suburb's streets echo the geography of Britain, with names drawn from English towns, counties, and rivers.
puzzles.reveal: It was Epping — where every street is a piece of Britain.

rounds.clue: I am the city that gave its name to a royal dukedom, a cathedral, and a famous cheese. What am I?
rounds.tidbit: Gloucester is home to the world-famous Gloucester Old Spot pig, known for its white coat with black spots.
rounds.explainer: Gloucester is a historic cathedral city in southwest England, on the River Severn. It was a key Roman settlement (Glevum) and later an important medieval trading hub. The city's cathedral, founded in 678 AD, is a masterpiece of Perpendicular Gothic architecture. Gloucester also gives its name to the traditional Gloucestershire cheese, a hard cow's milk cheese with a rich, tangy flavor.

rounds.clue: I am the longest river in the United Kingdom, flowing through both England and Wales. What am I?
rounds.tidbit: The Severn has the second-largest tidal range in the world, reaching up to 15 meters, creating the famous Severn Bore.
rounds.explainer: The River Severn is the longest river in the UK, stretching about 354 km from its source in the Cambrian Mountains of Wales to the Bristol Channel. It has been a vital trade route since Roman times, and its estuary is known for the Severn Bore, a tidal wave that can surfed. The river's name comes from the Latin 'Sabrina,' which has a legendary association with a mythical nymph. It flows through several cities, including Gloucester and Worcester.

rounds.clue: I am a rural county famous for cider, the Glastonbury Festival, and the legend of King Arthur. What am I?
rounds.tidbit: Somerset is home to the Cheddar Gorge, the largest gorge in the UK, and the original Cheddar cheese.
rounds.explainer: Somerset is a county in southwest England, known for its rolling hills, moors, and cider orchards. It is steeped in legend, with Glastonbury Tor linked to Avalon and King Arthur. The county hosts the world-famous Glastonbury Festival of Contemporary Performing Arts. Somerset's Cheddar Gorge is a limestone gorge that gave its name to the famous cheese, which has been made there for centuries.

rounds.clue: I am an eastern county of England, home to the Broads, a network of navigable rivers and lakes. What am I?
rounds.tidbit: Norfolk is home to the UK's largest seal colony at Blakeney Point, with over 3,000 seals.
rounds.explainer: Norfolk is a county in East Anglia, bordered by the North Sea. It is famous for the Norfolk Broads, a unique area of protected wetlands and waterways, created by medieval peat digging. The county has a rich maritime history, with ports like Great Yarmouth. Norfolk is also known for its windmills, which are iconic to the landscape.

rounds.clue: I am a county east of London, once a Saxon kingdom, and now known for my seaside resorts. What am I?
rounds.tidbit: Essex is home to the oldest wooden church in the world, St. Peter's Chapel in Bradwell-on-Sea, dating from 654 AD.
rounds.explainer: Essex is a county in southeast England, with a coastline along the North Sea. It was one of the kingdoms of the Anglo-Saxon Heptarchy, known as the Kingdom of the East Saxons. The county has a long history of agriculture and fishing, and in the 19th century it became a popular seaside destination. Today, Essex is known for its commuter towns and the historic town of Colchester, which was the first capital of Roman Britain.

puzzles.background: In a northern suburb of Melbourne, the streets pay homage to the legends of Australian cricket, each one immortalizing a player who left an indelible mark on the sport.
puzzles.reveal: It was Epping — where every street is a cricketer's tribute.

rounds.clue: His Test batting average of 99.94 remains untouched, a statistical marvel that has stood for over seven decades.
rounds.tidbit: Bradman was knighted in 1949, the first Australian cricketer to receive the honor.
rounds.explainer: Sir Donald Bradman is widely regarded as the greatest batsman in the history of cricket. His career spanned from 1928 to 1948, during which he scored 6,996 runs in Test matches. The infamous 'Bodyline' series of 1932-33 was specifically devised to curb his scoring. His legacy is so profound that the phrase 'Bradmanesque' is used to describe extraordinary batting performances.

rounds.clue: He spun the ball a mile and bowled the 'Ball of the Century' to Mike Gatting in 1993.
rounds.tidbit: Warne took 708 Test wickets, the most for Australia and second only to Muralitharan overall.
rounds.explainer: Shane Warne was a leg-spin wizard who revolutionized the art of spin bowling. He made his Test debut in 1992 and retired in 2007, leaving behind a legacy of 708 Test wickets. His charisma and skill made him a global superstar, and his 1999 World Cup-winning performance for Australia is legendary. Off the field, his life was equally colorful, filled with controversies and comebacks.

rounds.clue: A left-handed batsman from the 1950s, he was known for his aggressive strokeplay and was once called 'the best left-hander in the world' by Don Bradman.
rounds.tidbit: Harvey was the youngest Australian to score a Test century, at 19 years and 121 days.
rounds.explainer: Neil Harvey was one of Australia's finest left-handed batsmen, playing from 1948 to 1963. He was a key member of the famous 'Invincibles' tour of England in 1948. Harvey scored 6,149 Test runs at an average of 48.41, and his fearless approach made him a crowd favorite. He later became a respected cricket commentator and selector.

rounds.clue: He was the first cricketer to score 2,000 Test runs and take 200 wickets, a pioneer of the all-rounder's art.
rounds.tidbit: Benaud was also a legendary commentator, known for his dry wit and the phrase 'marvelous'.
rounds.explainer: Richie Benaud was a charismatic leg-spinner and captain of Australia from 1958 to 1963. He was the first player to achieve the double of 2,000 runs and 200 wickets in Test cricket. Benaud's tactical brilliance and showmanship made him a beloved figure. After retirement, he became the voice of cricket, commentating for decades with his distinctive style.

rounds.clue: He famously told England manager Pelham Warner during the Bodyline series: 'There are two teams out there; one is playing cricket, the other is not.'
rounds.tidbit: Woodfull was the only Australian captain to lead his team to a Test series win in England in 1934.
rounds.explainer: Bill Woodfull was the Australian captain during the controversial Bodyline series of 1932-33. He was a stoic leader who maintained dignity under intense pressure. Woodfull's batting was solid, and he later became a respected educator. His stand against Bodyline is a defining moment in cricket history, symbolizing sportsmanship over gamesmanship.

puzzles.background: In this northern suburb, the streets are named after British towns, counties, and rivers, creating a little map of England.
puzzles.reveal: It was Fawkner — where every street is a piece of Britain.

rounds.clue: I am the home of the world's most famous horse race, held on the first Saturday of November. What am I?
rounds.tidbit: The Melbourne Cup was inspired by the Epsom Derby, but Derby itself is famous for its silk mills and as the birthplace of the Industrial Revolution.
rounds.explainer: Derby is a city in the East Midlands of England, known for its role in the Industrial Revolution with the world's first factory, the Derby Silk Mill. It is also home to Rolls-Royce, which produces aircraft engines there. The name 'Derby' comes from the Old Norse for 'deer village'. Fun fact: Derby's football club is called the Rams, after the local regiment's mascot.

rounds.clue: I am a county on England's east coast, known for my flat landscapes, broads, and as the home of a famous fictional detective. What am I?
rounds.tidbit: Norfolk is home to the Broads, a network of navigable rivers and lakes, and to the village of Swaffham, where a famous witch was burned.
rounds.explainer: Norfolk is a county in East Anglia, bordered by the North Sea. It is known for its flat, fertile farmland and the Norfolk Broads, which are actually flooded medieval peat diggings. The county is also the setting for the detective novels of P.D. James, and it has a strong history of smuggling along its coast. Its name comes from the 'north folk' of the Angles.

rounds.clue: I am a town in Surrey, England, where the world's most prestigious horse race, the Derby, is run every June. What am I?
rounds.tidbit: Epsom is the namesake of Epsom salts, first discovered in a mineral spring there in the 1600s.
rounds.explainer: Epsom is a town in Surrey, England, famous for Epsom Downs, the racecourse that hosts the Epsom Derby, one of the world's most famous horse races. The town's name comes from a local chieftain named Ebba. Epsom salts, a compound of magnesium sulfate, were first crystallised from the mineral water there in the 17th century. The town also has a history of being a spa resort.

rounds.clue: I am a seaside district on the Wirral Peninsula, opposite Liverpool, where a famous ferry crosses the Mersey. What am I?
rounds.tidbit: Seacombe is one of the landing points for the Mersey Ferry, made famous by the song 'Ferry Cross the Mersey'.
rounds.explainer: Seacombe is a district of Wallasey, on the Wirral Peninsula, overlooking the River Mersey. Historically, it was a major ferry port connecting to Liverpool, with the famous Mersey Ferry running from its pier. The name 'Seacombe' means 'valley by the sea' in Old English. Today, it is a residential area with a promenade and views of the Liverpool skyline.

rounds.clue: I am a market town in Suffolk, England, with a medieval castle and a famous legend about a black dog. What am I?
rounds.tidbit: Bungay is said to have been terrorised by a phantom black dog, which appeared in storms and killed people in the 16th century.
rounds.explainer: Bungay is a small market town in the Waveney Valley of Suffolk, England. It has a ruined Norman castle and is known for the legend of 'Black Shuck', a ghostly black dog that reportedly attacked people in the church during a storm in 1577. The town's name come from the Old English for 'Buna's island'. It was once a centre for the printing industry.

puzzles.background: In this Victorian suburb, the streets are named after towns and landmarks from across England. Each road tells a story of a far-off place.
puzzles.reveal: It was Flemington — where every street is a British town or river.

rounds.clue: A famous white cliff stands here, and it's the closest point to the continent. Which town is this?
rounds.tidbit: Dover's white cliffs are made of chalk and rise over 100 meters above the sea.
rounds.explainer: Dover is a historic port town in Kent, England, known for its iconic white cliffs. It has been a key entry point to Britain since Roman times, with the castle dating back to the 11th century. The town is also the starting point for one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world.

rounds.clue: This city is famous for a cathedral and a medieval pilgrimage. Which one?
rounds.tidbit: Canterbury Cathedral is the mother church of the Anglican Communion and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
rounds.explainer: Canterbury, in southeast England, has been a pilgrimage destination since the murder of Archbishop Thomas Becket in 1170. The city's cathedral, founded in 597 AD, is one of the oldest Christian structures in England. It inspired Geoffrey Chaucer's 'The Canterbury Tales'.

rounds.clue: This town in Kent was once a major Royal Navy dockyard. Which is it?
rounds.tidbit: Chatham Dockyard built over 400 warships, including Nelson's flagship HMS Victory.
rounds.explainer: Chatham, in Kent, was a vital naval base for over 400 years, peaking in the 18th century. The dockyard's historic buildings are now a museum, and it played a key role in the Napoleonic Wars. The town also has connections to Charles Dickens, who lived nearby.

rounds.clue: This town is the headquarters of British horse racing. Which one?
rounds.tidbit: Newmarket has been a racing center since the 17th century, and its trainer-based yards are unique in the world.
rounds.explainer: Newmarket, in Suffolk, is considered the birthplace of organized horse racing, with records dating to the reign of James I. It is home to the National Stud and the Jockey Club, and hosts two major racecourses. The town's training grounds are a major economic driver, with over 3,000 horses in training.

rounds.clue: This market town in Surrey is known for its castle and proximity to the Hog's Back ridge. What is it?
rounds.tidbit: Farnham Castle has been a bishop's residence for over 800 years.
rounds.explainer: Farnham is a historic market town in Surrey, England, with a castle built in the 12th century. It was an important stop on the road from London to Winchester, the ancient capital. The town is also known for its Georgian architecture and as the birthplace of William Cobbett, a famous writer and politician.

puzzles.background: In this Victorian suburb, the streets pay tribute to the great wordsmiths of the English language, from Romantic rebels to colonial chroniclers.
puzzles.reveal: It was Footscray, where every street is a literary poet.

rounds.clue: He wrote, 'She walks in beauty, like the night' and died fighting for Greek independence.
rounds.tidbit: Byron kept a pet bear while at Cambridge, as college rules forbade dogs.
rounds.explainer: George Gordon, Lord Byron, was the archetypal Romantic hero—a poet, a rebel, and a celebrity. His scandalous affairs and revolutionary fervor made him infamous across Europe. He died of fever in Missolonghi, Greece, in 1824, while supporting the Greek War of Independence. His masterpiece, 'Don Juan', remains a landmark of satirical epic poetry.

rounds.clue: He wrote 'Ozymandias' and 'Ode to the West Wind', and his heart was reportedly snatched from his funeral pyre.
rounds.tidbit: After his drowning, Shelley's friends held a beach cremation; legend says his heart was plucked from the ashes and given to his wife Mary.
rounds.explainer: Percy Bysshe Shelley was a radical Romantic poet whose works championed atheism, free love, and political reform. He was expelled from Oxford for writing 'The Necessity of Atheism'. Shelley drowned at age 29 in a storm off the Italian coast. His poetry, including 'Prometheus Unbound', deeply influenced later generations, and he was friends with Lord Byron and John Keats.

rounds.clue: He wrote 'The Last Rose of Summer' and 'The Minstrel Boy', and his melodies were set to traditional Irish tunes.
rounds.tidbit: Moore's 'Irish Melodies' made him a national hero, and his poem 'Lalla Rookh' earned a fortune in its day.
rounds.explainer: Thomas Moore was Ireland's national poet, known for his 'Irish Melodies' that captured the spirit of a downtrodden nation. He was a close friend of Lord Byron and a celebrated wit in London society. His narrative poem 'Lalla Rookh' was a bestseller across Europe. Moore also wrote a biography of Byron, which remains a key source on the poet's life.

rounds.clue: This writer declared, 'There is no romance in the bush' — but he still made it the stuff of legend.
rounds.tidbit: Lawson's short story 'The Drover's Wife' is one of the most famous in Australian literature.
rounds.explainer: Henry Lawson was a bush poet and short-story writer who captured the harsh realities of Australian outback life. He was born in a tent on the goldfields and struggled with deafness and alcoholism. His works, like 'While the Billy Boils', are considered foundational to Australian identity. He is one of the few Australian writers to appear on a postage stamp.

rounds.clue: This writer's pen name was 'The Poet of the People', and he wrote 'The Man from Snowy River'.
rounds.tidbit: Paterson wrote 'Waltzing Matilda', which became Australia's unofficial national anthem.
rounds.explainer: Andrew Barton 'Banjo' Paterson was a bush poet, journalist, and horseman. He wrote 'The Man from Snowy River' and 'Clancy of the Overflow', celebrating the romantic side of rural life. His ballad 'Waltzing Matilda' is sung by Australians everywhere. Paterson also served as a war correspondent during the Boer War and World War I.

puzzles.background: In this suburban estate, the streets evoke the legendary court of Camelot, with names drawn from the tales of King Arthur and his knights.
puzzles.reveal: It was Glen Waverley, where the streets are steeped in Arthurian legend.

rounds.clue: I pulled the sword from the stone and united a kingdom. Who am I?
rounds.tidbit: Arthur's legendary sword Excalibur was said to have been given to him by the Lady of the Lake.
rounds.explainer: King Arthur is the central figure of Arthurian legend, a British leader who, according to medieval histories and romances, led the defense of Britain against Saxon invaders in the late 5th and early 6th centuries. His story, including the sword in the stone, the Knights of the Round Table, and the quest for the Holy Grail, has been told and retold for centuries. The historical existence of Arthur is debated, but his legend has become a cornerstone of Western literature and mythology.

rounds.clue: I am the legendary sword that grants its rightful owner the power to rule. What am I?
rounds.tidbit: In some versions of the legend, Excalibur's scabbard had the power to prevent its wearer from bleeding.
rounds.explainer: Excalibur is the legendary sword of King Arthur, often associated with magical powers and the rightful sovereignty of Britain. In most accounts, Arthur received Excalibur from the Lady of the Lake, although in earlier tales he pulled it from a stone. The sword has become a powerful symbol of justice and kingship, appearing in countless adaptations from literature to film.

rounds.clue: I was the greatest knight of the Round Table, but my love for the queen led to my downfall. Who am I?
rounds.tidbit: Lancelot's affair with Queen Guinevere is a central theme in Arthurian romances, often leading to the fall of Camelot.
rounds.explainer: Sir Lancelot, also known as Lancelot du Lac, is one of the most famous Knights of the Round Table, celebrated for his bravery and skill in battle. His illicit love affair with Queen Guinevere, King Arthur's wife, creates a tragic conflict that ultimately contributes to the downfall of Camelot. Lancelot's character embodies the ideals of chivalry, yet his human flaws make him a complex and enduring figure in Arthurian legend.

rounds.clue: I am the pure knight who alone achieved the quest of the Holy Grail. Who am I?
rounds.tidbit: Galahad was the son of Lancelot and was destined from birth to achieve the Grail due to his purity and virtue.
rounds.explainer: Sir Galahad, the son of Lancelot and Elaine of Corbenic, is renowned for his perfect purity and spiritual perfection. In Arthurian legend, he is the only knight worthy of finding the Holy Grail, a quest that symbolizes divine grace and redemption. His story highlights the ideal of knightly virtue, contrasting with the flaws of his father and other knights.

rounds.clue: I was the queen of Camelot, married to the king, and my love for a knight changed the fate of a kingdom. Who am I?
rounds.tidbit: Guinevere's marriage to Arthur was often seen as a political alliance, but her romance with Lancelot became legendary.
rounds.explainer: Queen Guinevere is the wife of King Arthur and a central figure in Arthurian romance. Her affair with Sir Lancelot is a pivotal element of the legends, leading to the fracturing of the Round Table and the eventual fall of Camelot. Guinevere is portrayed variously as a victim of circumstance or a tragic figure, and her story has been explored in many literary and artistic works.

puzzles.background: In this suburb, the streets evoke a map of Britain, with names drawn from English towns, counties, and rivers.
puzzles.reveal: It was Glen Waverley — where every street is a piece of Britain.

rounds.clue: This town's name is synonymous with a medieval castle and a famous 'Kingmaker'.
